overview: Otomí communities have a long history across central Mexico, with several languages and regional names, including Hñähñu. They did not form one unchanged kingdom. The broad 1492 to 1500 map label and the smaller 1530 to 1650 “Otomies” outline describe different areas and periods; this narrative also follows colonial communities around Guanajuato and Querétaro. Neither outline marks the full territory of today’s Otomí peoples.

periods.title: Earlier centres
periods.summary: Huamango’s terraces and ceremonial buildings offer one archaeological window onto Otomian communities.

periods.title: Communities with different alliances
periods.summary: Otomí inhabitants of the Tlaxcalan frontier resisted Cortés at Tecoac in 1519.

periods.title: Colonial settlement and frontier changes
periods.summary: Otomí-speaking communities moved and expanded in Guanajuato and Querétaro within a changing colonial frontier.

periods.title: Continuing regional identities
periods.summary: Language, family institutions and local traditions continue in diverse Otomí communities.

items.text: Huamango overlooks the Acambay valley from the San Miguel plateau. Builders levelled difficult ground and made broad terraces for temples and residential platforms. INAH identifies it as an Otomian settlement: a specific archaeological example, rather than the capital of every Otomí community.

Huamango’s pottery helps trace connections. Excavators provisionally distinguished an earlier phase with incense burners, braziers and burial vessels resembling material at Tula, and a later phase with comparisons to Teotenango and Calixtlahuaca. Similar objects point toward relationships; they do not by themselves identify a conquering army.

The sixteenth-century Huamantla Codex was painted on bark paper. It recounts a group’s migration from Chiapan toward Tlaxcala, encounters and battles, and later Spanish arrival and a church. Images preserve an Otomí account of place and history within the colonial period.

Conservators studying the Huamantla Codex identified cochineal red in sampled paint. Looking through a microscope at tiny pigment traces helps explain how artists made the manuscript, alongside historical readings of its pictures. Material analysis supplies evidence that a modern photograph alone cannot provide.

Otomí communities made different political choices during Spanish invasion. At Tecoac in 1519, Otomí defenders guarded a Tlaxcalan frontier and fought Cortés’s force. Elsewhere some communities allied with Spaniards against Mexica power. One ethnic label cannot stand for a single decision made by everyone.

The later map’s northern outline belongs in the history of a mixed colonial frontier. Crespo and Cervantes examine Otomí-speaking settlement in Guanajuato and Querétaro, including the Sierra Gorda foothills. Some Otomí leaders participated in conquest and settlement, creating communities within a changing colonial political landscape.

sections.title: Family work, food and sacred places

items.text: INPI emphasizes that households differ between regions: some are nuclear families, while others include extended relatives. Planting and harvest bring family members into shared work. Godparent relationships also create valued ties beyond a household, connecting families through religious and social responsibilities.

In the Mezquital valley, agave supported more than one craft. Its fibres supplied textiles, while its sap could be fermented into pulque. Fournier connects these activities with pottery for holding and processing sap, showing how a plant crop, containers and household work belonged to the same economy.

Working with scattered maguey plants also shaped where people lived. Fournier argues that their continuing care helped support permanent but dispersed settlements in the Mezquital. This is an interpretation of an economic landscape: a house did not need to stand in a dense city to belong to an organized farming community.

In the Tolimán area of Querétaro, Otomí-Chichimeca families maintain chapels devoted to ancestors. UNESCO describes annual journeys to sacred hills and Bernal rock, with ceremonies asking for water in a dry landscape. These are living local traditions with their own community setting.

Tolimán celebrations also involve chimales, large temporary structures made from reeds and leafy coverings. Their construction brings people together around an offering. A structure can be important even when its makers intend it to stand only for a celebration rather than for centuries.

“Ki hats'i” means “Good morning”. INALI prints it as a common greeting in Hñähñu of the Valle del Mezquital and credits Nicandro González Peña for the recorded voice. This is a modern, regionally identified language sample; other Otomí varieties can use different forms.

Otomí writing standards were developed with community representatives, teachers, activists, the Academy of Hñähñu Language and Culture, researchers and INALI. The participants came from several states. Agreeing how to write sounds can help people share teaching materials while recognizing regional diversity.

ending.text: Spanish colonial rule changed political relationships, settlement and landholding, without bringing all Otomí communities to one common ending. Languages, families and local institutions continue. The map cutoffs of 1500 and 1650 are coverage dates, not the disappearance of a people.
